Experimental Investigation, Data-Driven and Physics-Based Modelling of Bedform Dynamics in Alluvial Channels

Abstract:

Bedforms such as ripples, dunes, transitional forms and antidunes develop on mobile sediment beds and strongly influence flow resistance, sediment transport and channel evolution. Although the controls on bedform formation are well established, it remains unclear how geometry and migration vary across regimes under a common experimental protocol, and whether the aspect ratio (H/L) remains a reliable indicator near regime transitions. This study addresses these questions through a 50-run flume programme using two sediment sizes (d₅₀ = 0.38 mm and 0.75 mm) across a range of discharges and bed slopes, covering bed states from no motion through ripples/dunes, transition and antidunes. Pooling all regimes gave a weak height-length relationship (R&sup2 &asymp 0.33), while separating the data by regime gave much stronger fits (R&sup2 = 0.70, 0.98 and 0.83), showing that regime-wise treatment reveals scaling behaviour that a pooled relationship obscures. Migration velocity generally increased with transport stage, while the finer sediment migrated faster under comparable conditions and bed slope strongly influenced antidune migration. Building on these findings, the present study proposes three computational extensions: an interpretable machine-learning framework for bedform-regime classification and migration-rate prediction, a reduced-order Exner-based morphodynamic model, and generalized dimensionless relationships linking bedform geometry and migration to flow regime, sediment size and bed slope.
